When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”

Breaking: A Russian warship explosion in Benghazi, Libya engulfed the Steregushchiy-class corvette Merkury in flames, almost certainly destroying it.
A large explosion reported in the Libyan port of Benghazi indicates that a Russian missile corvette has almost certainly been destroyed. Flames engulfed the vessel although it is currently unclear whether it has sunk at its berth, ort merely been burnt out.
The Russian warship, provisionally identified as the Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corv e tte Merkury had been at the port for several days when the explosion occurred. The ship, nominally part of the Black Sea Fleet but currently operating out of the Northern Fleet bases in the Arctic due to the war in the Black Sea was escorting a convoy of ships. Those Russian government linked ships, similar to the Sparta II hit in the Baltic yesterday, are used for carrying arms exports.
Several sources seen by Naval News confirm the incident. Merkury can been seen on fire in multiple satellite images and other collaborating sources shared with us.
Merkury is the sistership of Boikiy which was, on 3 rd June 2026 seriously damaged by Ukrainian aerial drones (UAVs) in Veleshinsky drydock of the Kronstadt, St. Petersburg. The attack resulted in a powerful explosion and a huge fire which heavily damaged the ship’s superstructure.
The ship is almost certainly destroyed. Exactly how the explosion came about has not been reported, but Ukraine has been reported to be behind a number of successful attacks on Russian ships in the Mediterranean. On 23rd December 2024 the Russian government linked ship Ursa Major was sunk, likely by limpet mines. On 3rd March 2026 the LNG (liquified natural gas) tanker Arctic Metagaz was destroyed off the Libyan coast, likely by uncrewed surface vessels .

articles.title_orig: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.title_zh: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.content_orig:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.
At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.
The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.
So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?
Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.
On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire , as it thwarted several other attacks that day.
The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.
The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.
Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.
Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.
Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.
Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.
Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.
Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.
Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.
According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.
Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.
The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.
About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.
Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.
Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.
Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.
As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.
The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.
The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.
Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.
Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.
“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.
The ongoing US naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and a wave of new sanctions imposed in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast are hurting Iran economically.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran, has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure.
The strikes on US interests in the Gulf in recent days have therefore been viewed as a defiant response to the US campaign. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Trump may choose to declare victory and walk away from the war on Iran rather than negotiate a deal, but continuing the naval blockade on Iran would risk further military escalation, says Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Parsi said Trump was unlikely to accept an agreement that could be seen in Washington as showing the war had failed.
“If he continues the blockade, there will be escalation,” Parsi warned, arguing that Iran would not refrain from retaliating against continued economic pressure.
He said Trump would need to “slowly, perhaps imperceptibly, lift the blockade, as well as lift some of the sanctions” if he wanted to withdraw from the confrontation without renewed fighting.
Hassan Ahmadian, professor at the University of Tehran, said Iran is forcing a “binary” choice on Trump.
If Washington lets the tankers pass, the US blockade “ends without an agreement or war”, Ahmadian said on X. However, if the US attacks the vessels, it could face “Iranian responses that will be difficult for [Trump] to avoid”.
Trump said on Saturday he had plans to make a deal with Iran that is “permanent” and prevents it from getting a nuclear weapon.
He also told US broadcaster Fox News that he was never very interested in regime change in Iran, but called its new leadership “more rational”.

Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU.
At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."
May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."
May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union.
Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations.
The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.
Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government.
"It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want.
"And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.
"When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."
Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head.
"He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer.
"Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."
Speaking to the BBC back in 2023 , she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".
Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.
May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.
On Saturday, Sir Tony Blair - another former prime minister - weighed in on the UK's future relationship with the EU.
Speaking to The Sunday Times , Sir Tony has said Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.
Sir Tony, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."
But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.
Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.
It comes after Burnham struck a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme .
The prime minister also said that over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for their long-term relationship.
He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.
However, Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship still on fire off Finland after attack
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship still on fire off Finland after attack
articles.content_orig:
A fire on board a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones off the coast of Finland in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, the Finnish coastguard said.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remains at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic’s stock market debut turned the vast majority of the young startup’s staff into overnight millionaires — some many times over.
The company’s headcount stood at 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. After Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, about 600 employees entered the rarefied “centi-millionaire” club, with equity holdings valued north of $100 million, according to data from Hill.com , which tracks private-company shares.
As many as 2,800 staffers, known internally as “Ants,” have holdings valued above $10 million. And about 5,100 — 96% of the staff — are sitting on equity north of $1 million.
“What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Andrew Benson, Hill’s founder and CEO, told CNN on Thursday, noting Anthropic has seen very little attrition. “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.”
Anthropic valued at $1.76 trillion after first day of trading
It’s not unusual for Silicon Valley startups, which are typically light on cash, to pay their staff with a combination of salary and stock. The promise of a future acquisition or initial public offering tends to keep workers motivated to work hard and stick it out until payday.
But few startups have grown as big or as quickly as Anthropic. The company, founded in 2021, had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024.
As with most tech startups, Benson noted, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.”
SpaceX, by contrast, spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster IPO in June. That debut minted around 4,400 millionaires, out of a staff of 22,000.
Anthropic’s IPO is also unique for allowing non-founder insiders to cash out on Day One of trading. In most IPOs, staff are subject to a “lockup” period — typically three to six months — during which they can’t sell their shares. But Anthropic’s listing included a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as the stock began trading. (It’s not known how many insiders may have taken advantage of the opportunity Thursday.)
And unlike SpaceX, which has employees spread across Texas, California and Florida, Anthropic is uniquely concentrated in San Francisco, a city whose entire economy has been reshaped by sudden surges of tech wealth.
A rash of newly minted millionaires could soon amplify pressure on San Francisco’s housing market, where home prices are already rising at their fastest pace in years.
The typical home there sold for $1.7 million in October, up nearly 19% from a year earlier, according to Redfin. By contrast, the national median home price was roughly flat over the same period, at $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.
CNN’s Samantha Delouya contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.title_zh: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.content_orig:
Pain, swelling, and stiffness in the knees can be downright debilitating.
As cartilage breaks down in these joints, it can significantly reduce freedom of movement and cause pain, even when standing still or sitting.
Surprisingly enough, core exercises may be a neglected form of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
A randomized controlled trial in India has now found that working out the abdominal muscles may have a trickle-down effect for the knees.
Strengthening the abdomen won't stop cartilage from degenerating, but in this particular trial, when core exercises were added to typical rehabilitation programs, it improved physical function more than conventional exercises alone.
What's more, patients who did the core exercises also reported significantly less pain when moving about.
The findings are published in Scientific Reports , and while the study is small, the methodology was rigorously designed.
The trial involved 100 participants, aged 40 to 80, with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis.
Roughly half the group were randomized to partake in conventional knee-focused rehabilitation for 12 weeks.
During the trial, this half of the group partook in 45 minutes of supervised exercise three times a week for four weeks.
Each session involved progressive strengthening, range-of-motion, and functional exercises, such as straight-leg raises and moves to strengthen the quadriceps.
Participants then continued these exercises at home on their own for an additional 8 weeks.
Meanwhile, the other half of the group was randomized to undertake a different rehabilitation program.
This one involved a mix of conventional knee-based rehabilitation exercises and progressive core-targeting exercises.
The core exercises included abdominal bracing, glute bridges, forearm planks, arm raises while lying down, heel taps, and alternating arm-and-leg movements similar to dead bugs.
After the 12-week intervention period, both groups demonstrated significant reductions in resting pain.
But it was the group that also partook in core training that demonstrated greater improvements in physical function tests and reported less pain when moving about.
Importantly, this group also reported greater improvements in their quality of life.
The authors of the study don't know why core training led to these benefits, but they suggest that an improvement in posture control may help stabilize the body's core during exercise, putting less strain on the lower limbs.
"Collectively," the team concludes , "these biomechanical adaptations provide a plausible explanation for the greater improvement observed in pain, physical function, and quality of life compared with conventional knee-focused strengthening alone."
The findings are supported by previous research, which also suggests that the core is a neglected part of knee pain.
In 2021, for instance, a peer-reviewed narrative review argued that despite preliminary findings that core training is beneficial for knee issues, more research is needed.
"Investigations that show it is safe and effective in older adults have not been adapted to/incorporated into treatment recommendations for those with knee osteoarthritis," the authors argued.
This year, the results of several randomized clinical trials have begun to roll in.
One trial among 48 patients with knee osteoarthritis in Pakistan, for example, also found that adding core stability training to knee exercises produced greater improvements in pain, knee mobility, and quality of life after 12 weeks.
Plus, a larger study of 100 patients found that adding core exercises to conventional knee rehabilitation was more effective than adding foot-and-ankle strengthening.
That seemed to be particularly true for outcomes like pain and physical function.
Related: Study of 33,500 CT Scans Challenges a Common Assumption About Ab Strength And Back Pain
These randomized trials are small, but their findings suggest that exclusively targeting the joints during osteoarthritis treatment may not be the best move.
The whole body is connected, and the function of our extremities is founded upon the stability of our trunk.
Ab exercises may help cut to the core of the issue.
The research has been published in Scientific Reports .

This story is part of a WSJ series on aging. A new piece will publish each day through Dec. 1.
Baby boomers have transformed every demographic they aged into. Now they are trying to redefine old age .
This year, the oldest boomers are turning 80 and the youngest ones will be eligible to claim Social Security . They are living longer. They are more educated than prior generations and many of them are well-off.
This group of 76 million babies born between 1946 and 1964 is a massive generation. They grew up in an era of post-World War II prosperity and upward mobility, against the backdrop of the Civil Rights Era and President John F. Kennedy’s assassination. As adults, they changed societal norms by living in dual-income households, getting divorced, traveling the world , and investing in the stock market en masse.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq Turns Red For The Year
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq Turns Red For The Year
articles.content_orig:
Esteemed Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel was more animated than usual on Friday afternoon... with good reason.
The normally staid author of "Stocks for the Long Run" spoke to CNBC on Friday as the market careened toward some ugly milestones. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory, off more than 10% from their records. The Nasdaq Composite lost its gain for the year and the more concentrated Nasdaq-100 entered bear market territory on an intraday basis.
"These things are like straws that break the camel's back. You know what I mean? Everyone [is] all, 'I don't care, I don't care cause everything else is good' and when those straws keep on going... Bang," said Siegel.
Just a month-and-a-half ago, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were at record highs. But the straws were already adding up by then and a market in denial is just now recognizing them.
Here are the reasons behind the sell-off:
The breaking point came this week in the form of the initial public offering of artificial intelligence leader Anthropic and a pick-up in the selling intensity for one-time AI chip leader Nvidia.
Anthropic upped its offering amount a day before going public despite the already dimming climate around AI-related stocks. The move ensured it would be the biggest IPO ever, but played into the fears that this debut — following SpaceX's monster offering over the summer — was a collective cash-out moment for the AI complex that will leave the investing masses holding the bag.
In other words, it could be the ultimate "sell the news" moment for the AI trade.
On Thursday, Anthropic traded from its $83 IPO price to a high above $115 before instantly rolling over and taking the AI trade with it. Anthropic's sell-off intensified Friday, and when the dust settled Anthropic closed the week at $88.91.
The Nasdaq posted its worst week since the Covid plunge of March 2020, down 10%.
Nvidia fell 14% on Friday with the selling intensifying after a Reuters headline hit the tape that the chipmaker's accounting is the focus of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe.
Nvidia is now down nearly 40% in November alone, a month that saw the AI bull market's leading salesman, Jensen Huang, resign as its CEO because of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy that raised speculation about whether the company's chips were ending up in Beijing's hands despite government restrictions.
To start the week, the Commerce Department tightened restrictions on U.S.-made chips to stop China from accessing them remotely from other countries.
A solid earnings report on Tuesday fell flat as Nvidia's board definitively ruled out any chance Huang would return, disappointing some of the stock's fanatics still holding out hope for his far-fetched return. Nvidia ended the week with a 23% loss.
The S&P 500 traded below its 200-day moving average — what's considered a measure of a security's long-term trend — on Tuesday and made a convincing break of it on Thursday. This turned many on Wall Street— like commodity trading advisors — into automatic sellers on the market. So-called CTAs are individuals or organizations that advise others on trading futures and swaps across a range of assets.
"We know there's a lot of trend riders on these markets," said Siegel. "They have their trend lines. They've ridden it up and as soon as it goes down, they're selling and they're selling and they're selling and they just perpetuate" the decline, he said.
The Iran conflict has caused the price oil to surge and while it's off its highs it still remains above $83 a barrel, while the fees for transiting the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the region keep persistent pressure on global prices.
A series of numbers earlier in the month showed inflation is still far from the Federal Reserve's 2% target, sparking a run of central bank officials to warn they may have to get more aggressive with interest rates.
After increasing rates in September by a quarter point, the Fed skipped a hike in late October and sparked concern among bond investors it may be falling behind the inflation fight. The 10-year Treasury yield subsequently jumped above 5% and stayed there until a flight of safe haven fixed income buying brought it back below that level on Friday.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said this week that the Fed may need to do a half percentage point hike next month to catch up.
"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC.
"Don't fight the Fed" has long been a maxim on Wall Street and right now expectations are that the central bank will need to raise rates in December and again in January.
And late-breaking on Friday was a report from the Financial Times that the Trump Administration is considering restarting strikes on Iran .
Before the grim market milestones were met on Friday, it had long lost its mojo on fears that the pace of growth driven by AI companies was slowing.
As Anthropic prepared to go public, its third-quarter figures released earlier this month showed revenue growth last quarter was 47%, down from 144% in the second quarter.
AI momentum trades, like the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF , all topped out during the summer.
The fears of slowing growth picked up this month after the Democrats won control of Congress and key governorships, fueling speculation that states — or even the whole country — could implement stricter rules on data center construction.
CoreWeave , which builds data centers using high amounts of debt, is down 71% from its high. Caterpillar , which has reinvented itself as an AI play because of data center construction and generators, is down more than 50% from its high.
The view of Siegel and many market observers is that the economy remains in good enough shape that this will just be a run-of-the-mill correction that resets a bull market that had raised people's expectations too high because of its early ferocity.
The S&P 500 returned more than 20% in 2023 and 2024 and then gained 16% last year.
"The average over long periods for the stock market is 8%, 9% a year up," said Siegel. "People began to think that 15 to 20 [percent] was going to be the norm with AI and we have to bring that down to reality."
"Stay with your stocks,' he said.
The only problem with that theory is that the stock market and its wealth effect was one of the major factors underpinning the economy. Stocks are a greater source of household wealth — especially for baby boomers — than they ever have been before.
With the S&P 500 clinging to a 1% gain for the year, this stock market rout could end up tipping off a virtuous cycle that slows the economy, and in turn, leads to bigger equity losses.

articles.title_orig: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.title_zh: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.content_orig:
Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument
The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.
The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.
Despite mounting pressure, an agreement to discuss an instrument to regulate autonomous weapons over the next two years fell short of the urgent action rights groups said was needed to address the looming threat.
“We’re starting to see artificial intelligence … being fielded in the battlefield and perhaps also already in weapon systems. If we leave this unregulated, it will be much more difficult to put the genie back in the bottle,” said Dr Cordula Droege, the director of international law, movement and partnerships at the ICRC.
Autonomous weapons are military systems that act without human supervision, often through the use of artificial intelligence or other forms of robotics.
As artificial intelligence has grown exponentially in recent years, militaries and manufacturers have created increasingly advanced weapons systems for both offensive and defensive purposes.
These systems include the use of AI in generating target banks , as was done by the Israeli military in Gaza, as well as semi-autonomous drones in the Ukraine-Russia war, which have “last-mile capability”, where AI takes over in the drone’s final approach to its target.
The president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, and the UN secretary general, António Guterres, have called for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on use of weapons. In particular, the ICRC has called for a ban on the use of autonomous weapons against personnel, as well as ensuring that weapons systems behave predictably and placing limits on weapons including restricting their use to military objectives.
Experts have said that given the rapid development of autonomous weapons and AI, the failure to create adequate regulations could have dangerous repercussions.
“It’s not about banning all autonomous weapon systems, but to set limits in an international treaty of red lines that should never be crossed,” said Droege. “We’re very close to crossing those red lines, particularly targeting human beings through machines should be a moral red line.”
Other rights groups warned that any delay towards regulation of these weapons risked allowing private industry and militaries to set the norms of how autonomous weapons are used.
Already, autonomous weapons have led to civilian harm. Three civilians were killed by a Russian drone guided by an AI system in July in Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine. The drone tried to hit a petrol station, probably its intended target, but instead crashed into a wall, killing three people in a fountain of shrapnel.
In Gaza, Israel has used AI-assisted targeting methods to fill its target banks much faster than humanly possible since the start of the war. As a result, rights groups have said that civilians and people with tenuous links to militant groups were erroneously killed.
In Iran, a US strike that hit an elementary school, killing 156 civilians including 120 schoolchildren, reportedly was a result of faulty intelligence gathered by AI systems.
Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said further delay to a strong treaty could see “more cases of mass civilian harm that we’ve seen over the past 18 months to two years”, warning that some of these mass casualty events could dwarf what has already occurred. She said manufacturers and militaries were trying to develop “swarm” capabilities, where hundreds or thousands of autonomous drones act at the same time.
“This has the potential for high damage, just because of the sheer mass of systems that would be autonomous. All it takes is for one of them to face algorithmic error and then the entire swarm is utilised and led down a path based on that error … particularly if they’re programmed to target humans.”
There is also a risk of proliferation, as non-state groups increasingly use AI to program their weapons systems, as was the case when the Houthi movement in Yemen used Claude to “vibe code” ballistic missiles.
Armed Islamist groups in Africa’s Sahel region have reportedly used AI tools to improve drone ballistics and for operational planning.
“This is the only thing that is important this week. It’s not really the substance of laws. What’s on the agenda here, after 13 years, is the political will finally present to start to get serious about regulation of autonomous weapons systems,” said a senior diplomat with knowledge of the UN discussions.

articles.title_zh: What to know about US-China competition as Trump and Xi meet again this week - Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe

SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes.
As they dispersed to their capitals, the presidents had few tangible gains to show for a summit hastily assembled in a matter of weeks, bypassing the months of groundwork that typically underpin diplomatic breakthroughs.
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking, a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to journalists.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
But if any substantive understandings were reached behind closed doors, none of them were released to the public.
The summit’s pageantry fit a familiar pattern for Trump, who has repeatedly staged headline-grabbing encounters with controversial leaders only to walk away empty-handed. Three high-stakes meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term failed to meaningfully shift relations between Washington and Pyongyang, and a meeting with Putin in Anchorage last year likewise failed to generate progress toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
This time, the spectacular gathering lasted just an hour and a half, and produced only a readout of four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically, overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against the Islamic Republic this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the start of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that [Putin] and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since their summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in the Republican president’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with  Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.

articles.content_orig:
Leonida, an open source project aimed at statically recompiling the console version of Grand Theft Auto VI for Xbox Series X into a native OS application, has appeared on the GitHub platform. WindowsSince the console processor uses the x86-64 architecture, the authors of the initiative translate the console system calls into the PC environment, and translate the compiled RDNA2 graphics programs into the SPIR-V format for operation via the API. VulkanThe project is distributed under the GPL-3.0 license and does not contain any copyrighted game files, encryption keys, or executable modules. To build the port, the user will need an unpacked copy of version 1.0.2.1 of the game, from which the utilities will automatically extract the necessary assets and generate shaders locally on the computer.
At this stage the game does not launch yet, as the developers lack an executable file to complete the work on the loader and the D3D12 graphics layer for VulkanHowever, the toolkit already successfully extracts and converts all 26 game shaders to SPIR-V, as well as exports 503D models to OBJ format, textures to DDS, and audio tracks to Ogg Opus or WAV. Building the project independently on a PC requires certain software and hardware requirements.
The automated build script automatically finds the game folder on local drives using the MicrosoftGame.Config configuration, checks for the presence of the required components, and saves the finished result in the user's documents directory. WindowsThe process of resource extraction and shader validation is supported on Linux, where the executable loader can be launched via Wine or Proton. The project's repository already has over 8,2 stars and 147 contributors, who continue to refine the translation of graphics commands and the emulation of 64-thread shader groups for NVIDIA and Intel graphics cards.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s AI resistance: workers ready for battle over data centres
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s AI resistance: workers ready for battle over data centres
articles.content_orig:
Angela Huffman , a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH , and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH , sheep farm.
On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky.
The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town.
"We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com® . Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant.
"What does that do to the community?" she says.
Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures.
Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone.
Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment blocking large data centers within the limits of the 6,600-person town.
"They wanted to use about a third of the water the whole town uses today," Huffman says. "I'm not against AI or development, but can a town of this size absorb a development like that?"
But the state already hosts dozens of large centers. And they already exact a cost.
A new study shows that the state's data center tax break derived its schools of almost $374 million in revenue in 2025 alone.
Republican Gov. Mike DeWine paused the tax breaks in May after the state realized developers were exempted from $2.1 billion in taxes in 2024 and 2025, far more than initally projected. Gov.-elect Amy Acton has promised further scrutiny.
Good Jobs First and Policy Matters Ohio studied where those missing tax dollars would have gone. The state's Fair School Funding Plan allocates some sales tax to schools. So by exempting data center developers from the 5.75% sales tax, those schools missed out on revenue.
“Ohio lawmakers made a choice to give data center companies a blank check, and now Ohio’s schools are paying the price,” said Hannah Halbert , Policy Matters Ohio’s executive director. “In 2025 alone, the state gave up enough revenue from this single tax break to fully update the Fair School Funding plan and close the gap.”
This comes at a time when homeowners were being asked to make up the difference. Many Ohio schools aimed to raise money through levies this year, but many were unsuccessful. The Ohio Policy Education Institute found just 24 of 66 levies on the May 2026 ballot had passed.
Upper Sandusky's school district was one of the losers—missing out on $383,000 in revenue, according to the report. While voters have approved levies for its schools in 2015, 2018, and 2023, it's still been forced to cancel classes this year because it can't install air conditioning in century-old buildings that are too expensive to rebuild.
"Our schools were struggling," Huffman says. "It tells you a lot about when these big tech companies come along, and if they are paying their fair share."
Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. NBC exit polls show 76% of voters opposed data center building in their communities, and a majority considered them "crucial" to their votes.
Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs , raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.
That's despite a major spending spree by the industry. Ohio was barraged with $1.8 million in data center ads in the fall, Pew Research Center found—more than Texas , Wisconsin , and other large states. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million backing Republican Sen. John Husted , who lost reelection to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3.
Developers, after all, have big plans in the state, having pitched $168.7 billion in new projects.
Regulation of data center developments and AI could be a major factor for new Democratic leaders in Columbus and Washington , DC. Sober to that reality, tech stocks tanked after the election .
Acton says she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers. She wants to see them cover their utility costs, build with union labor, and abide by environmental standards. She also says she wants to see incentives "reined in" for the large developments.
Artificial intelligence companies have spent the days since the election promising they'll work with cities and residents on data centers. OpenAI published a " blueprint for responsible development " promising to slow the technology.
Meta spokesperson Andy Stone cited a commitment "to pay our own energy and water costs so they're not passed onto consumers, fund new and upgraded grid infrastructure, and support local communities."
Ohio isn't alone, either. Virginia , another data center hot spot, spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. It and other hot spots like California and Texas have also moved to restrict data center developments this year.
A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also said that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.
Ohio, in the meantime, has seen its housing situation worsen in the past few years. National Housing Conference data put the state first in the union for how quickly middle-income earners have been priced out. The number of jobs that can afford a typical home at a 10% down payment fell about 41% from 2020 to 2025. Teachers, firefighters, and retail supervisors are among those priced out of median-priced homes.
But data center advocates say the large developments are still necessary in the modern economy.
Dan Diorio , vice president for public policy at the Data Center Coalition, told the Ohio Tax Credit Authority that the developments benefit all people and businesses, not just AI companies.
"This is a far more efficient way of doing all the computing, processing, and storage that we need to facilitate our daily lives in the 21st century economy," Diorio said at the May hearing in Columbus. "The need for connectivity, for the internet, is driving the digital infrastructure that supports that."
Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title_orig: Mike Waltz warns Russia faces ‘unsustainable’ losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
articles.title_zh: Mike Waltz warns Russia faces ‘unsustainable’ losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
articles.content_orig:
US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz warned Friday that Russia is suffering “unsustainable” battlefield losses, with monthly deaths outpacing recruitment numbers.
Speaking on “ The Brian Kilmeade Show ” podcast, Waltz echoed President Trump’s assessment that Russian President Vladimir Putin is “worn down,” arguing the war in Ukraine cannot be won militarily and must end at the negotiating table.
“Right now, the numbers that we have, the Russians are recruiting 20,000 to 25,000 a month of new fresh recruits,” Waltz said. “They’re losing 30,000 to 35,000 a month, dead every single month.
“That is exponentially more than they lost in Afghanistan and approaching what they lost in World War II, a thousand a day,” he added. “It’s just unsustainable.”
The interview followed Trump’s return from Shenzhen, China, where he met with Putin before joining the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping for the first-ever three-way summit between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China.
The summit produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but the leaders stopped short of announcing breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran.
At a White House news conference Friday, Trump addressed questions about Putin’s intent regarding the war.
“He’d love to end the war. It’s a very hard thing to do,” Trump said Friday. “To be honest, you have two guys that don’t know how to end it. We’re trying to help them.
“You have two people that hate each other, Zelenskyy and Putin. They don’t know how to end it. They want to end it. They’re both stuck in it,” he added. “And it’s a horrible war, actually. And I thought it would have been maybe one of the easier ones to get ended. But the personalities play.”
Waltz argued that both Ukraine and Russia have “worn each other down,” saying it’s unlikely the two countries will be able to sustain the current level of fighting.
“It’s a horrific war, and the president remains determined to find some construct of a deal that will end it because neither side can sustain this war of attrition,” Waltz said. “There is no winning it militarily. It’s got to end diplomatically.”
Fox News Digital’s Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Is Blowing Away Gaming's Greatest Devs, Including Naughty Dog
articles.content_orig:
Naughty Dog’s Michael Barclay – whose credits include Uncharted: The Lost Legacy and The Last of Us 2 – says he’s “made video games for 19 years and GTA 6 appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child”.
Rockstar’s latest open world release is by far the best-looking game ever made, even if it is locked to 30fps on PS5 hardware .
And it’s being treated like witchcraft by devs, who naturally have a greater appreciation for the feats on display.
Barclay, who’s currently working on next year’s Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet , continued :
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
“I'm always astonished that [Rockstar’s] environmental lighting is mostly dynamic and looks as good if not better than most baked lighting.”
In really, really simple terms, baked lighting is a game development technique used to save computational cost by calculating light and shadow data in advance.
The downside to this is that it’s fixed, but obviously given the ever-changing nature of GTA 6’s sandbox, it needs to have a dynamic solution.
Barclay is saying that GTA 6’s dynamic lighting matches and even surpasses those pre-determined solutions in many scenarios, making it a real accomplishment.
These comments triggered discussion from various other industry professionals, including Tim Soret from Odd Tales, the makers of The Last Night , who outlined some of his thoughts on the title:
GTA 6 sets a standard so unfathomably high I do wonder at what point it’ll ever be topped.
I suppose raising the bar like this will motivate the many other talented devs around the world, but not every studio will have access to the time and the estimated $1 billion budget that allowed Rockstar to deliver this.
Either way, it’s clear industry professionals are utterly blown away by what the studio has delivered here.

Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

articles.content_orig:

United Nations climate talks in Turkey have approached a final deal as COP31 presidents hope to finally achieve consensus on how to advance the fight against global warming.
COP31 president Murat Kurum told a late-night plenary session: “We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” as the conference was set to reconvene on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts warn of the need for urgent and deep cuts to emissions, mainly from the use of coal, oil and gas. The world is already on track to blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperature.
Civil society organisations wrote to Cop31 ’s joint presidents, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum, overnight to tell them they had hours left to avoid making it “one of the most disappointing Cops [the UN] has ever had”.
“The Global South is being abandoned,” they said. “Developed countries have blocked progress across the negotiations and arrived with no new finance commitments.”
Negotiators ran past a Friday deadline, straight through Saturday and into the early hours of Sunday. Their new version of the deal text refined an earlier draft, which had been heavily criticised by some for lacking ambition because it contained no reference to ending the use of fossil fuels.
Kurum has said he felt concerns around fossil fuels had been addressed, as had those around helping developing countries finance their adaptations to climate change.
Delegations have until 3am GMT to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 6am GMT to begin approving it.
Australia led the talks with Turkey, which is hosting the meeting, and nearly 200 delegations from the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations. It was hoped that a year of climate disasters could help sharpen minds at the conference.
Devastating floods in Mozambique flooded more than 150,000 homes and killed at least 22 people. Coming off the back of other climate disasters in the country - including Cyclone Kenneth in 2019, as well as a crippling drought across 2023 and 2024 - charities told The Independent they were struggling to attract donors due to foreign aid cuts.
In August, after a piece of melting glacier dislodged high up in the mountains, devastating floods in Nepal caused an estimated $4.8bn in damages, and left 1,500 dead and 10,000 injured.
There is also the threat a record breaking El Nino weather event that the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) has projected that an additional 49 million more people could be pushed into hunger globally.
A climate “loss and damage” fund was established at Cop27 in Egypt in 2022 in order to provide developing countries with compensation for climate disasters. But it has so far secured just $822m in pledges, and countries affected by climate disasters are limited to apply for only $20m per disaster – less than half a per cent of Nepal’s needs.
“Nepal did not create the climate problem. But we keep being hit by massive floods, not just this year but also in 2025, 2022 and other years,” said Bisesh Sangat, a Nepali attendee of Cop31 who works for the NGO Practical Action. “There’s a lot of big infrastructure losses, but also the human losses mean that you go to villages and there are lots of widows and children without fathers, so the losses are very profound.”
There was already deep disappointment after a draft published on Thursday afternoon failed to include any mention of fossil fuels - despite the fact that this had previously been mentioned in the outcome of Cop28 in Dubai in 2023.
This cover decision is seen as the key outcome of the UN climate conference, and is set to be a key signal that countries will take home and implement in national policy.
Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank said: "If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost COP. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here. After the progress made in 2023 at Cop28 in Dubai where fossil fuels were mentioned for the first time, there is now no mention of the f-word at all. Cop31 has been muzzled on the most important threat causing the climate crisis."
Stories emerging from the negotiating room suggest that the usual suspects were to blame for an outcome that was less ambitious than hoped. Saudi Arabia has been among the main objectors to any wording on the “transition away from fossil fuels”, with insiders suggesting that the world’s largest oil exporter played a key role in blocking ambitious language.
Pelin Zorlu, senior research fellow lead on climate and energy at the Chatham House think tank, said: “The Cop Presidency has acknowledged the difficulty of reaching consensus on fossil fuels, with opposition from the Arab Group, Russia and others.”
But others pointed their fingers at the EU for not being ambitious enough, particularly around Turkey’s high profile pledge to raise electricity's share of total final energy consumption from around 23 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035. Such a move makes sense if the electricity is powered by renewables – but not if it is done so with coal.
Laurie van der Burg, from NGO Oil Change International, said: “The EU is trying to shift blame onto others and it is deeply hypocritical. At the beginning of Cop31, it signalled it was prepared to drop the renewable energy sources ask from the electrification target and it has failed to put forward an EU fossil fuel transition roadmap. Even worse, the EU blocked progress on the public finance, adaptation, and just transition that developing countries urgently need. These are not side issues. They are essential to making a fair fossil fuel phaseout possible and protecting communities from climate disasters.”
At the same time, the EU and other wealthy democracies have expressed dismay at receiving too much blame when it is they who are providing the bulk of climate finance - and especially so with the US absent. EU member states provided €32.3bn in public “climate finance” in 2025, which mobilised a further €9.3bn in private finance.
There is growing disquiet that the group of countries who are required to provide this “climate finance” – crucial capital needed to decarbonise and adapt to climate change – is fixed around a list of developed countries that was devised in 1992, known as “Annex II”. It means that newly-wealthy countries, including China, the UAE, South Korea and Singapore, do not officially have to provide climate finance, while the likes of Greece and Portugal are required to.
While plenty of lobbyists were in attendance, one group was conspicuously absent: world leaders. Neither China’s Xi Jinping or India’s Narendra Modi, or any hint of the US federal government made an appearance – with Andy Burnham the only G7 leader in attendance. Yet, while powerful countries fight it out, ultimately it is the world’s most climate vulnerable countries who are losing out.
On Friday afternoon, Ghana's minister for environment, science and technology, Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings did not mince her words.
Africans were being “excluded by the use of technicalities, with the use of inaccessible finance, and with the use of shifting goalposts and lack of commitment and delivery on promises… Africa is not a continent merely seeking assistance. We are asking the developed countries to keep promises that they already made.”
In what seemed to be a reference to the US, she said: “There are countries who from the onset decided not to be a part of this agreement. There, they were plain and honest… What we do not appreciate are those who choose to remain a part of the framewor
