articles.title_orig: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.title_zh: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.content_orig:
Over the past few years, Apple has improved how much users can customize their iPhone Lock Screen. Initially, the company only allowed changes to the background wallpaper. Then, how it showed wallpaper when the screen dimmed. Now, the lock screen works with customization widgets, allowing you to add and change many aspects of what the iPhone's Lock Screen can do . You could tweak the clock, the wallpaper, fonts, and add color filters. Suddenly, there were widgets and Live Activities too. The latest iOS 27 update, which comes with the all-new Siri AI, also included more customizations to the clock and widgets, allowing you to make the iPhone look more your own.
Interestingly enough, Apple's great revamp on iPhone customization started with iOS 18 , which coincides with the moment the company should've made available all the Apple Intelligence features we are only seeing now. The company had already begun offering ways to change the lock screen with widgets, filters, and new fonts. With iOS 18, Apple added those features to the Home Screen, and Control Center, while making more refinements to the lock screen too.
After that, Apple brought the Liquid Glass design language with iOS 26, which gave the iPhone's software a visual overhaul. As of 2026, Apple's included improvements like animated album covers from Apple Music on the Lock Screen, access to up to three Live Activities in the Dynamic Island, and more.
All that change is a lot to keep track of. So here's an easy list of the best ways you can customize your iPhone Lock Screen to look cooler.
If you're running iOS 27 and have access to the new set of Apple Intelligence features thanks to the new Siri AI, one of the coolest things you can do is to extend your wallpaper on the Lock Screen. For example, if you have the perfect photo, but it's in landscape orientation, or you don't want your partner's or pet's face too zoomed in on your Lock Screen, here's what you can do: After long pressing the Lock Screen > Adding/Customizing a Lock Screen , you can zoom out the image until the iPhone gets an "Extend" feature. Using on-device AI, the iPhone will recreate a part of the image to make it fit the vibe you're going for.
Once you do that, you can customize other parts of your Lock Screen. If you have an iPhone with the Action Button and Camera Control functionalities, for example, you can remove the traditional Flashlight and Camera widgets to something else you might want to access faster, if these options are redundant to you. There's a number of shortcuts you can choose from, including Apple options and third-party apps. Et voilà, you have the most original Lock Screen possible.
Another cool feature introduced with iOS 27 is the opposite of what previous software brought. While the Lock Screen clock was getting bigger over the years, now you can make it smaller to give it a very minimal aesthetic look. Just tap on the clock while editing, and then on the upper right of the font options is a button that looks like two rectangles. Tap it, and your clock will shrink into the date area.
Another important tweak that few people actually take advantage of is Apple's Focus Modes. Introduced in 2021's iOS 15 update , Apple lets you create different Lock Screen, Home Screen, wallpapers, and filters for different parts of your day or mood. You can create one for work, and another for while you're in the car. If you're at swim practice, you can set another wallpaper and only allow specific people to call you, etc.
Mastering Focus Mode can take a while because it has so many potential combinations of its features, but the outcome can be very rewarding. Many people use it to avoid getting those endless social media notifications during work hours, or even prevent Trello and Slack from buzzing you when you're long gone from your work. Did I mention these Focus Modes can be set up by location? Since your phone knows where you are, the Focus Modes can trigger when you get to or leave a specific place, by a specific hour, or even when Apple Intelligence understands you're doing something else — like when you start playing a game or commuting on the bus.
You can find Focus Modes by opening the Control Center and venturing inside the Focus tab. With that, you can go beyond the Do Not Disturb option and create different filters for the day, including unique Lock Screen combinations that make sense for that specific moment of the day.
Another cool feature for someone who wants a completely different Lock Screen wallpaper is to create AI-generated wallpapers based on your photos, or memoji, or even just a prompt you give about a visual you're imagining in your head. When customizing a Lock Screen , tap the Plus button , then Image Playground , select between a few design styles, and then describe an image for a unique wallpaper. A bonus tip is that with iOS 27, you can even remove the Now Playing card from the Lock Screen, and whatever is playing will continue to play, bringing the ultimate minimalist design.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Is Racing to Keep Its Booming Defense Industry From Stalling
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Is Racing to Keep Its Booming Defense Industry From Stalling
articles.content_orig:
“If China were to decide to restrict its exports, Ukraine as well as the rest of Europe and the US would feel that immediately,” says Igor Nakonechnyi. The CEO of Project Foundation, a Ukrainian bid to build chip capacity in Europe, tells EU Perspectives why the drone industry depends on China and what Europe can learn from Ukraine’s frontline.
The war in Ukraine has exposed how heavily the world’s drone industry relies on China for critical components . The Fourth Law is a Ukrainian defence technology company that develops autonomous drones for use on the battlefield.
Together with its sister company Odd Systems, which supplies drone cameras, it is working to establish semiconductor manufacturing capacity in Europe through an initiative called Project Foundation. The two firms want to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers and address a vulnerability that affects Ukraine’s drone industry and Europe’s wider security.
In the interview, Igor Nakonechnyi describes the daily struggle to source components amid sudden shortages and price hikes. He also explains why the company is opening an R&D hub in Eindhoven, why many EU funding programmes take too long to pay out, and why the Chips Act should cover dual-use technologies.
Our company was created in response to Russian aggression. Our team already had quite some experience in entrepreneurship and consumer electronics, so they were looking at how they could best use their skills in the face of the aggression.
Drones are a defining feature of modern warfare. One of the key components of a drone is a camera. Basically, they are the eyes of the drone.
The real bottleneck here is the thermal sensor — a semiconductor chip that allows a camera to detect heat. China can make around 20 million of those a year. Every thermal drone needs a sensor, so whoever controls sensors controls how many thermal drones can be built.
Outside China, it is pretty much only North America and France that have some manufacturing capacity, which is maybe a couple of million in total. That’s a huge discrepancy, and we see it as a huge vulnerability.
Indeed. If China were to decide to restrict its exports, Ukraine as well as the rest of Europe and the US would feel that immediately.
Even if we haven’t yet seen a full restriction, there’s already always a shortage of specific things, or the price suddenly goes up. — Igor Nakonechnyi, CEO of Project Foundation
Even if we haven’t yet seen a full restriction, there’s already always a shortage of specific things, or the price suddenly goes up. It’s a constant challenge that our procurement team deals with on a daily basis.
That’s a critical vulnerability that we want to solve not only for Ukraine, but also for Europe and the rest of the world. That’s exactly why we launched Project Foundation, to build thermal-sensor fabs in Europe and the US, so the West no longer depends on China for the eyes of its drones.
We are currently setting up a subsidiary in the Dutch city of Eindhoven, where Project Foundation is headquartered and will serve as one of our main R&D hubs.
We see ourselves as part of Europe. And we see a lot of opportunities and talent in Europe to build this with.
I see that a lot of relevant stakeholders already understand this, and more and more are becoming aware. In the US, even more so: more money is being invested in sovereign production, specifically of military equipment. This has always been the case, but investment is growing even more now. In Europe, it’s gradually getting better.
To be clear: my company does not receive any EU funding at the moment. But we are looking at a few funding calls.
However, we see that many funding programmes have timelines that are simply too slow for us. If you want to apply for funding, it can easily take a year before you actually get it. So you need to write a project, wait almost a year until you get the money, and then you have two or three years to build a prototype.
Even within a year, warfare in Ukraine will have changed completely, and the concept you requested funding for might no longer be relevant. — Igor Nakonechnyi
That timeframe doesn’t match modern warfare. Even within a year, warfare in Ukraine will have changed completely, and the concept you requested funding for might no longer be relevant.
There are more agile programmes coming, but we need more of them. We really need more speed.
Yes, that’s a very good initiative, but a big problem for us is that it’s primarily for civil use and not dual use. For example, what we are working towards—thermal-camera sensors or image sensors—is not really part of the Chips Act, whereas we believe it is an important topic.
We are talking about semiconductor manufacturing here, so it makes sense from that perspective. We do already see dual use in, for example, the Industrial Accelerator Act [a proposed EU law aimed at boosting manufacturing and demand for European-made and low-carbon products].
The reality of today’s world is that many different things are interlinked. Embracing dual use in, for example, the Chips Act would reflect that reality.
Our company is originally driven by demand in Ukraine, but we of course want a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. And that peace only lasts when there’s a strong, independent defence industry behind it to deter another war. We hope to continue contributing to that; not only for Ukraine but for the wider Western world.
We see ourselves as a global company, and also hope to use our products in civilian applications in the future, such as consumer robotics and cars. We don’t want this to end up only in the hands of China.

articles.title_orig: Trump opens door to bipartisan deal on credit card rates as Americans face record debt
articles.title_zh: Trump opens door to bipartisan deal on credit card rates as Americans face record debt
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates , hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers . The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push . Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."
Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.
"The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley posted on X on Saturday.
Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

Ferrari unveiled the 296 Challenge Stradale and 296 Challenge EVO, two new cars developed in close collaboration to highlight the symbiotic bond between the Prancing Horse's race cars and production cars, as well as the exceptionally high level of technology transfer that sets them apart. The 296 Challenge EVO builds on the car that redefined the standards of the Ferrari Challenge and will make its debut in the 2027 season, while the 296 Challenge Stradale brings the technical essence and pursuit of uncompromising performance to a road-legal vehicle.
The cars were unveiled during the 2026 Ferrari Finali Mondiali, held at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya in Montmeló. The final event of the Prancing Horse's racing season brings together, on the same track, the Ferrari Challenge, programmes dedicated to competition cars and non-competitive activities.
The 296 Challenge Stradale is the Ferrari currently in the range that can offer the most direct link to a race car. The car is indeed stripped-back, almost clinical in its setup, entirely geared towards providing the driver with a direct and physical driving experience. Performance, consistency, and repeatability of driving characteristics thus become the defining characteristics of its dynamic setup.
The 296 Challenge EVO, on the other hand, builds on the strengths of the 296 Challenge with the aim of boosting absolute performance without compromising driveability and consistency. The versatile aerodynamic package, improved dynamic controls, and wider operating range make the car faster, more predictable, and more consistent, bringing the driving experience even closer to that of the 296 GT3 Evo.
Both feature the 2,992 cc 120° Ferrari twin-turbo V6 engine in the exclusively internal-combustion configuration of the 296 Speciale, which has received numerous accolades and rewritten lap records at circuits throughout Europe. In the 296 Challenge Stradale, it develops 670 hp at 8,000 rpm and is paired with an eight-speed dual-clutch F1 transmission; in the 296 Challenge EVO, it instead delivers 700 hp at 7,500 rpm, with a specific output of 234 hp/l and a seven-speed F1 transmission. The absence of a hybrid component limits the car's weight and complexity, further underscoring the direct connection between driver and accelerator, engine, and rear wheels.
The 296 Challenge Stradale has a dry weight of 1,330 kg, a full 140 kg less than the 296 GTB, and boasts a weight-to-power ratio of 1.98 kg/hp. The 296 Challenge EVO shares the same weight, underscoring the fact that both cars have been designed with a focus on lightweight construction and performance.
This approach is also evident in the design. The volumes and surfaces of the Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale have been stripped of superfluous elements to reduce the car's visual mass and make its technical functions more readily apparent. The result is a deliberately more essential and racing-inspired design language, in which every element serves a purpose and helps distinguish it from the other berlinettas in the range. The car thus retains its visual connection with the 296 Challenge EVO, reinterpreting it in line with the safety, type-approval, and practical requirements specific to a road car.
Aerodynamics represent one of the principal points of contact between the two cars: the 296 Challenge Stradale generates 617 kg of downforce at 250 km/h, 72% more than the 296 GTB, through an integrated system comprising a fixed rear wing, splitter, flick, aero damper, vortex generators, and a fully enclosed underbody.
The 296 Challenge EVO increases maximum downforce by 12% compared with the 296 Challenge, equivalent to an additional 100 kg at 250 km/h, and introduces the Low Drag configuration, which reduces minimum drag by 4%. The difference in aerodynamic load between the High Downforce and Low Drag setups has more than doubled. The wider wing adjustment range, the Low Drag kit, the redesigned rear diffuser, the new mirrors, and the carbon-fibre components extend the 296 Challenge EVO's operating window across different circuits. A high-performance driveshaft with dedicated cooling broadens the component's operating window under the most demanding conditions. The option to increase rear ride height by up to 10 mm provides approximately 30 kg of additional downforce at 250 km/h.
The vehicle's dynamics follow the same philosophy of maximising performance. The 296 Challenge Stradale features ABS Evo in all driving conditions and in every Manettino setting, along with specific control systems, a dedicated setup, and Pirelli P Zero R and P Zero Trofeo RS tyres. The 296 Challenge EVO updates its traction-control and electronic-differential control strategies to improve combined performance, braking stability, and agility through high-speed corners; the new brake-pedal curve also increases modulation, travel, and pedal load at the same level of deceleration.
The 296 Challenge EVO improves consistency over race distances and reduces tyre degradation. In comparative testing, the car proved faster on the circuits analysed, with an improvement of 0.8 seconds at Mugello compared with the 296 Challenge. The redesigned instrument cluster makes driving information, control intervention levels, TPMS data and lap times easier to read. These features are particularly significant in the run-up to 2027, when the Ferrari Challenge will introduce three rounds featuring 40-minute Endurance races, beginning with the second event of the season at Mugello, which will mark the debut of the new format.
The engine retains the 120° twin-turbo V6 architecture in the 'hot-V' configuration first introduced on the 296 GTB. articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates , hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers . The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push . Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."
Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.
"The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley posted on X on Saturday.
Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title_orig: UN climate talk negotiators go into second day of overtime while at odds over fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: UN climate talk negotiators go into second day of overtime while at odds over fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.
Nations were deadlocked in Turkey on how to advance the fight against global warming, after new draft agreements included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
A third and "final" text was sent to delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning and members had until 06:00 local time (0300 GMT) to raise concerns before a 9am local time (0600GMT) meeting for approval.
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended to reconvene next year.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said.
"We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
If the countries can't agree, the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year.
This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".
France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture - a technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground.
She said it was being used as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Another key issues raised by developing nations is the the lack of money.
Another sticking point involved a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptations to climate change, however the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

Considering the gap between the first and second-gen Moto Tags, we weren't expecting Motorola to launch Moto Tag 3 anytime soon, but it seems Motorola could launch it in a few months, or even weeks, as it is already listed on Amazon.
Amazon UK has listed the Moto Tag in Pantone Lucent White color, while Amazon Italy has listed the Pantone Indigo Blue version. If both listings are to be believed, the Moto Tag 3 will be hardly different from the Moto Tag 2, as it looks identical and shares the same features.

Amazon states the CR2032 cell will provide more than 500 days of battery life on the Moto Tag 3, which is the same as the Moto Tag 2 . However, Motorola's US and UK websites list the Moto Tag 2 as having more than 600 days of battery life.

With more than 500 days of battery life powered by a replaceable CR2032 battery, it is designed for long-term use. The model number mentioned in the Moto Tag 3 images on Amazon is XT2561-1. articles.title_zh: Intel Nova Lake-H Spec Sheet Shows Up With a 4.8 GHz Boost and 25 W TDP
articles.content_orig:
We finally got a glimpse of one of the upcoming 16-core Nova Lake mobile chip, and what it brings to the table.
Here is one of the early appearances of one of the upcoming Intel Core Ultra 4 series processors. Thanks to @momomo_us, we got a glimpse of a Nova Lake-H mobile processor on an Advantech board (for robotics and industrial applications), which is going to power the next-gen mainstream mobile devices. The specs sheet doesn't mention the SKU model name, but it mentions "Core Ultra Series 4" and "Nova Lake-H" as the codename.
The specs sheet details most of its specifications, including the core configuration, cache size, memory support, and TDP rating. The processor uses an 8P+4E+4LPE configuration, combining eight performance cores, four efficient cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Even though this is the same configuration as the 16-core Nova Lake-S processor we reported on previously , this one is specifically for the mobile platform.
The processor is expected to carry the Coyote Cove architecture for the P cores and Arctic Wolf E cores as previously reported. The 16-core Nova Lake-H leaked SKU is reportedly featuring a good 4.8 GHz Turbo clock, 2.0 GHz base clock, and 18 MB of LLC cache. The page also mentions its integrated graphics configuration, which reportedly features a 2.3 GHz clock speed. However, details like execution units and architecture are missing.
It's expected that the Nova Lake-H SKUs will have integrated Arc graphics based on the Xe3P architecture and will carry up to 12 GPU cores for the higher-end variants. This might be the one that carries the 12-GPU-core configuration, but we will wait for official confirmation. One more interesting detail here is the memory support. The processor reportedly supports DDR5-8000 MT/s and up to 128 GB of capacity. This aligns with our previous reports that suggested a good 800 MT/s jump over Panther Lake, which supports DDR5-7200 MT/s.
Another key detail is the power rating, as the leaked specs reveal the SKU reportedly runs at a 25W TDP. This is well below the power range expected from the Nova Lake-S desktop processors, for which vendors have started introducing PSUs with three 8-pin EPS connectors .
The leaker @momomo_us also spotted a Nova Lake-S listing on the OpenBenchmarking platform. This is an early Nova Lake-S sample with 28 Cores and up to 5.2 GHz turbo boost. This is likely the 8P+16E+4LP-E configuration chip that could carry a 296W PL2 limit .

articles.title_zh: The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.
articles.content_orig:
President Trump on Friday signed the Common Cents Act , which lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law.
It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents. For example, if a purchase costs $10.02 after tax and a customer is short 2 cents, the tab would round down to $10 under the act. A charge of $10.04 would round up to $10.05.
Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor.
Business advocacy groups cheered its passage. NACS, which represents the convenience and fuel retailing industry, said it creates reliable guidelines for conducting cash transactions.
"Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended," Brennan Duckett, NACS' director of regulatory and policy, said in a statement to CBS News. "NACS members benefit directly from this law, and we are pleased to see President Trump make it official with his signature."
Business owners said they faced confusion and were vulnerable to litigation before the act passed.
"As a retailer, I am grateful to have established legal guidance on rounding cash transactions," Scott Zietlow, CEO and president of Kwik Trip, said in a statement Friday. "Every cash transaction that we processed in recent months was a reminder that we needed more clarity from the federal government. We've now got that clarity."

articles.title_orig: Russia Says Cargo Ship Attacked By Drones in Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russia Says Cargo Ship Attacked By Drones in Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.title_orig: EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October
articles.title_zh: EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October
articles.content_orig:
High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!
This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash. The overall market dropped 27% year over year (YoY), to around 1.6 million sales. Plugins were down 14% YoY, but pure ICE sales were much worse off, crashing 44% YoY!
Adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug! If this trend continues in the future, the Chinese market will be fully electrified by 2030, and will be 100% BEV before 2035!
This great result pulled the 2026 share up, to 59%, already 5% above the full year result of 2025. BEVs on their own were up to 40% (versus 33% in 2025).
At this pace, I expect the final number for 2026 EV share in China to be above 60%, with BEVs alone north of the 40% mark. And when the largest global automotive market gets this electrified … then the ICE industry is in serious trouble.
The ICE extinction is also visible in the overall ranking. The overall top 10 was fully made by EVs. Again.
Looking at the best sellers in several size categories , the ICE extinction is also quite visible. Although, once again, the C-segment/compact category is the exception, with the only ICE representative showing up there — the Toyota RAV4, in 2nd, behind the leader Nevo Q05 and just ahead of the BYD Dolphin.
Having a quick look at the five size categories, the highlight is the B-segment/subcompact category, which is the hottest segment right now, with three of the top four top sellers in October belonging to this category.
Considering that 56% of the new SUVs launched this year were bigger than 5 meters/197 inches, there is a clear disconnect between what people want (small hatchbacks/crossovers) and what OEMs offer (large SUVs).
Another highlight is the fact that Xiaomi had a gold plus silver win in the full size category, with the BYD Great Tang closing out the podium while the midsize category podium was 100% BYD Group.
Here’s more info and commentary on October’s top selling electric models:
A BYD Dolphin for BYD Seagull money ($10,000) . This was Geely’s internal memo to describe the formula for the Geely Xingyuan when developing its star model. With an interesting name — Xingyuan translates as “wishing upon a star” — it seems that Geely had its wish granted. However, the Geely model will have a tough adversary soon, as the new generation Seagull will land with only one goal — to steal the Xingyuan’s best seller status. But while the new Seagull didn’t land, the small Geely scored a record performance in October, with its 50,190 registrations representing a 14% increase YoY. Besides the new BYD Seagull, Geely’s hatchback now has to deal with Leapmotor’s B-segment contenders, the A10 and A05; the new-generation Wuling Bingo; Chery’s new QQ3; and let’s not forget about BYD’s Yuan Up, too.
BYD’s midsize SUV continues to transition into the new generation. Thanks to the ramp-up of the new Ultra body, BYD’s star player was 2nd, scoring 30,772 registrations . Sales were up by 6% compared to the same month last year. The new Ultra generation features lidar and 1,500 kW DC charging, and these two features aren’t even the most impressive aspects of the model! That would be the price. It starts at 152,000 yuan (or $22,000) with the 76 kWh battery, and it goes up to 180,000 yuan (or $26,000) with the 83 kWh battery. For comparison, the Tesla Model Y starts in China at 259,000 yuan ($38,250)…. Expect the Song to experience a second youth from here onwards, and while it is impossible to displace the Tesla Model Y from the runner-up spot, the last place on the podium is doable this year. And maybe higher up in 2027?
BYD’s small crossover continues to surprise, thanks to recently improved specs. BYD’s team player rose to 3rd in October, scoring 28,514 registrations , which was a 44% increase YoY and a new record score. Despite not being the most exciting vehicle to look at, or drive, the truth is that it is surfing the wave of small, affordable EVs better than most, scoring high in value for money with prices starting at $11,000 and higher end versions having BYD’s driver-assistance system. With small vehicles currently having a moment in China, expect the small crossover to show up in the top 5 more regularly.
Things continue to go well for the startup brand, with its new baby A10 now established as the star player in an already strong lineup. Thanks to 27,247 registrations , the small crossover managed another top 5 presence. The model has the usual value-for-money focus of the brand, and a low, low price of 66,000 yuan ($10,000). On top of that, however, the A10 offers something close to a distinct personality, as the design eschews the white product standard design of Leapmotor for something more personal, mostly thanks to the front and back lights and a floating roof effect. With B-segment BEVs now being the hottest category in China, Leapmotor is well prepared to benefit from the subcompact rising tide, thanks to the recent arrival of the A10 small crossover and its sibling, the A05 small hatchback. Talk about perfect timing….
After the SU7 and YU7, Xiaomi has another success on its hands. This big fat SUV — or shall I say SUVs, as the lineup is broken down between the 7-seat N90 and the 5-seat N70 — scored 27,132 registrations in only its second month on the market, pulling it immediately into the overall top 5. Even with the number of competitors growing every passing day, Xiaomi’s new land yachts have been selling like hot cakes, while drying up sales of the competition. Proof of that, is the fact that there were only two full size models in October’s top 20, with the other being … the Xiaomi SU7.
Looking at the rest of the best seller table, there were a number of models hitting record scores, starting with the #8 Nevo Q05 (20,022 units) continuing its success story. The #10 Bestune Xiaoma (17,887 units) benefitted from a recent refresh to score a surprise record score. Could this mean that small city EVs are (finally) seeing the light at the end of the tunnel?
As for the second half of the table, the highlight is the ramp-up of the Xpeng L03, with the attractive looking crossover, which kind of reminds of a mini-Lotus or small Polestar, reaching 13th thanks to 15,653 sales. This EV looks to be the startup’s star model thanks to a competitive price (124,000 RMB) that is half the price of the Tesla Model Y!
Other models with record performances were the #14 MG 4 (15,503 units), with the new generation proving to be much more popular and adaptable to local tastes than the previous one, and the #17 Chery QQ3 EV, which continued its slow climb in the ranking thanks to 14,041 sales, which made it the 5th B-segment model in the top 20.
Still in the top 20, we should also highlight the best selling foreign model, the Tesla Model Y VW ID.Aura T6 , the new China-made (and China-developed) German crossover that has allowed Volkswagen to beat the Texans for the first time in years (the Tesla Model Y was down 60% YoY, to 7,807 units, while the Model 3 was down 85%, to 1,010 units). The Aura T6, VW’s take on the Model Y formula, rose to the 20th position in its first full month on the market!
A promising sign, or just hype? Only time will tell, but at least for now, VW seems to be getting some traction on the EV side of the Chinese market, a point also highlighted by the fact that it wasn’t just the Aura T6 getting decent sales. The also new VW ID.Era 5S (think Chinese VW Jetta) got 7,100 registrations in October. Is there hope after all?
Outside the top 20, the main event was the ramp-up of Nevo’s new baby, the Q06, which is looking to replicate the Q05’s success in the category above. With some 10,000 registrations in only its second month, it looks like it could join the top 20 soon. The same can be said about the Geely Galaxy TT, the make’s answer to the Xiaomi S

articles.title_zh: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.
The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators to discuss Iran negotiations
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators to discuss Iran negotiations
articles.content_orig:
Iran says Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran as the country’s foreign minister urges the United States to accept Iranian conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
News of the talks came as the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) toured an underground missile facility on Saturday and the country’s president said Iran is facing a “silent economic war”.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night and held two hours of talks with Iranian officials, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said, according to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy,” he said on Saturday.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. ⁠The conflict has drawn in countries across the region, disrupted shipping and ⁠pushed up global energy prices.
Gharibabadi said the talks have not yet become formal negotiations. If they do, the technical details of Iran’s nuclear programme would be discussed, he added, but Iran’s position is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country.
He also said Iran regards the US economic blockade as an act of war and will “take any action necessary” to break it.
For his part, US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a “permanent” deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are “very, very difficult”.
“We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he added.
The ongoing talks in the region “must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, according to state television.
“Our position is clear: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” he said.
“At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves.”
Iran’s conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Araghchi also said reopening the strait is “not difficult”, and requires the US only to “accept reasonable conditions that are in accordance with international law”, Tasnim reported.
The minister said there is “no solution” unless Washington acknowledges its mistakes and fulfils its previous commitments.
Iran has restricted shipping through the strait, which normally carried about a fifth of the world’s oil, since the war began. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports in response.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that his country is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles”, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian told a meeting of investors and producers that “a group of bullies, oppressors, and coercers sought to bring down our country”, but that Iranian businesses had managed market conditions well.
He said the government was working to avoid power cuts over the winter.
Meanwhile, IRGC commander Major-General Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility, accompanied by Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, who heads the IRGC Aerospace Force, Tasnim reported.
Vahidi was briefed on the force’s readiness and recent developments in its missile programme.
The visit follows the Aerospace Force’s unveiling of a new underground facility earlier this month, where it displayed ballistic and cruise missiles and their launchers, Tasnim said.

articles.title_orig: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.title_zh: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.content_orig:
A survey of AI proxy services suggests stablecoins have become a key payment rail for Chinese users accessing restricted US models
Sat 21 Nov 2026 · 10:35 EST · 2 min read
Every time a major US AI lab ships a new frontier model, a shadow market on the other side of the Pacific starts paying up. In stablecoins.
That is the core finding of a new report from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. It found that payments from wallets suspected of links to China jumped 55% above baseline within three days of key US AI model releases.
Export controls were meant to keep advanced American AI out of reach. Instead, they appear to have created demand for a middleman economy, and crypto is helping settle the bill.
The report, published on November 21, 2026, describes a market where Chinese users reach restricted US frontier AI models through proxy or agent services. These services act as go-betweens, offering access that export controls would otherwise block.
Chainalysis surveyed 100 of these service providers. Of those, 40% accept payment in crypto, with stablecoins doing most of the work.
The timing pattern is what makes the data stand out. Activity from suspected China-linked wallets did not just drift upward over time. It spiked right after new US models dropped, which Chainalysis read as a sign of a coordinated rush to tap the latest capabilities.

Chainalysis described an ecosystem with increasingly specialized roles.
Access suppliers provide the underlying connection to US models. Brokers connect buyers to that access. Payment processors handle the money side of the transaction.
Some of those payment players go a step further. According to the report, certain processors obscure stablecoin transactions by routing them through third-party channels, making the trail harder to follow.
The economics help explain why. Chainalysis noted that paying for proxy access is cheaper than training comparable models from scratch. Users can query US models and distill those capabilities into local systems, essentially learning from the output rather than building the foundation themselves.
The AI findings build on earlier Chainalysis work. A report released in October 2026 had already flagged a significant rise in peer-to-peer stablecoin transactions from China-linked wallets, despite domestic restrictions on crypto trading.
That October report recorded $104.1 billion in self-custodied stablecoin transfers from China-linked wallets. Those transfers came across 18.1 million transactions between July 2025 and June 2026.
Over the past year, the Chinese crypto ecosystem has been estimated at at least $176 billion. Peer-to-peer activity accounted for 59.1% of that total.

articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_zh: Galaxy S27 Release Date: Early Software Reveals iPhone-Style Overhaul
articles.content_orig:
A new leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.
Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers , rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.
Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.
SamMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.
The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.
When this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That update is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.
What do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

articles.title_orig: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.title_zh: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.content_orig:
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
after newsletter promotion
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.content_orig:
Stocks got hit hard this week amid fears that the AI trade could be buckling. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters .
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race .
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness .
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.

articles.title_orig: UK maritime agency reports two tanker incidents near Oman; Iran says vessel hit mine east of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: UK maritime agency reports two tanker incidents near Oman; Iran says vessel hit mine east of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.title_zh: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent AlpÃ¶ge said , external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday , external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths , external and physics , external .
A group of maths scholars said , external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released , external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.
